key_insight: In peer-to-peer health narratives, factual agreement with medical consensus does not reliably indicate safety; risk and truth can be largely independent.
clinical_relevance: Systems that only check whether online health advice is factually correct may still miss harmful guidance or unnecessarily suppress safe but unconventional content.
method: Analyzed 704 health narratives (699 classified) using two non-overlapping scores: Narrative Truth Distance and Narrative Risk Score.
Compared how epistemic divergence and health risk relate across narratives and mapped them into a four-quadrant governance model.
Tested benchmark performance on 437 expert-labeled posts with 127 misinformation instances, including supervised, frozen-embedding, and prompted-LLM approaches.
evidence_signal: Truth and risk shared only 4.9% of variance (r = 0.222, p < 0.001), and the best benchmark discrimination reached Youden's J = 0.349.
watch_item: The study is based on specific narrative and benchmark datasets, so the quadrant framework should be validated before being used to drive real moderation or clinical policy decisions.
paper_title: The Online Health Safety Gap: Consensus Alignment Does Not Imply Safety in Peer-to-Peer Health Narratives.
